source.title: Evidence against Learned Search in a Chess-Playing Neural Network

page_placements.theme: Decision-relevant state and policy across layers in chess and agentic models (state tracking, not shown look-ahead)

record.tranche_reason: The post reports its own analyses of Leela Chess Zero and argues that the results are more consistent with pattern recognition than substantial deliberate look-ahead.
record.gate_note: The post cites another paper's findings and includes predictions and interpretations in the comments; these are not recorded as study results. The overall first-move solve rate measures chess capability, not the presence of look-ahead, so it is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The post runs its own behavioural analyses of Leela Chess Zero's policy and value outputs on 1895 single-winning-move composition puzzles. It argues the results fit multi-move pattern recognition rather than substantial look-ahead. These results bear on V5 (look-ahead in chess) and V6 (heuristic explanation). The analysis is indirect: it uses output patterns, not internal representations.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author also argues it can be ruled out that a substantial part of Leela's puzzle prowess comes from deliberate calculation. He says transfer to LLMs is unclear because they are not limited to a single forward pass.
record.recipe_differences: Uses chess-composition puzzles and Leela's move predictions and value estimates, rather than the cited paper's interpretability analyses of future-move representations and interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Puzzle mate depth, whether the puzzle was solved, and material balance are analyzed as varying conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Leela predicts the correct first move on a bit more than 50% of 1895 single-winning-move composition puzzles.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Leela's policy solves a substantial share of out-of-distribution chess composition puzzles from the first move.

record.problems: The post says the analysis cannot rule out a mixture of pattern recognition and look-ahead. It does not report uncertainty estimates, and the dataset is filtered to puzzles with one winning move; the author also notes that transfer to language models is unclear.

untested.parts: Multi-step reasoning and Sokoban. Internal representations of future moves in chess (no interpretability probes or interventions).
Token look-ahead horizon in language models. Local next-token features in LMs. Whether chess plans steer generation causally.

missing.what: Per-depth solve rates and winning probabilities, and material-balance curve values, shown in figures but not quantified in the text
missing.locator: Analysis results — Accuracy by depth; Winning probability by material balance (figures)

record.verdict_notes: Each row's single state is relative to V5. For V6 (the challenge version) the same rows read as observed. In the comments, Erik Jenner (an author of the cited paper) argues these puzzles are too hard and unfiltered, so first moves may be found by luck. That is a reason the results may not transfer to the paper's filtered setting. The value-head measures are confidence outputs used as indirect evidence, not direct measures of internal look-ahead. This is a LessWrong post with no uncertainty estimates or controls.

versions.untested_parts: Rhyme-word representations and interventions on rhyming verse.
Decodability of future tokens from a hidden state.
Pre-caching or breadcrumb features in language models.
Rhyme planning in open-weight language models.
Only the chess aspect is examined. Multi-step reasoning and Sokoban are not tested.

The post examines a pattern-recognition explanation versus substantial deliberate calculation in chess. It does not measure a token look-ahead horizon or test local next-token features in a language model.

relationships.condition: Leela network on Schwalbe composition puzzles with one winning move, judged by policy/value output patterns
relationships.reason: Several behavioural signatures of look-ahead fail to appear on this puzzle set. Deeper mates are solved more often (r2), confidence does not vary with depth (r3), and there is no confidence jump when solved (r5). Value also collapses with unfavourable material despite the correct move (r6). The author concedes a mixture is possible, so look-ahead is limited here rather than refuted.
relationships.display_finding: Deeper mates were solved more often, confidence neither varied with depth nor jumped when solved, and value collapsed under unfavorable material despite correct moves, although these patterns left a mixture involving look-ahead possible.
